title: Records and SQL
specPoints: 2.2.3 **Records** to store data; **SQL** to search for data: `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, with `*`, `AND`, `OR`, `LIKE`, `ORDER BY`
Read, write and correct simple SQL queries on a single table
learn: Explain what a record is and how a table is a collection of records with fields
Write `SELECT … FROM … WHERE` queries that return the right fields and rows
Use comparison operators, `AND`/`OR`, wildcards with `LIKE`, and `ORDER BY`
Read a query and state what it returns
Spot and fix errors in a query (wrong field, missing quotes, wrong operator)
hook: You want every student in Year 10 who scored over 70 in the mock, sorted by surname. In Python that's a file, a loop, a split, an if, a sort — twenty lines. In SQL it is one sentence. Databases are where most of the world's data lives, and SQL is how you ask them questions.

video.title: SQL in one lesson: SELECT, FROM, WHERE
video.brief: 4 minutes. A table `Students` drawn as a grid: rows highlighted as records, columns as fields. `SELECT *` lights the whole table; `SELECT Name, Score` dims other columns; `WHERE Score > 70` fades rows out; `AND Year = 10` fades more; `ORDER BY Surname` shuffles rows into order; `LIKE 'A%'` keeps names starting with A. End with the three mistakes: missing quotes round text, `=` with `LIKE`, comma after the last field.

p: A **record** is one set of related data about one thing — one student: ID, name, year, score. Each piece is a **field**. A **table** is many records with the same fields; in Python you might hold a record as a small list or a dictionary and a table as a list of records. A **database** holds tables and lets you query them with **SQL**.
explain.code:
Students
StudentID | FirstName | Surname | Year | Score
----------+-----------+---------+------+------
1         | Ada       | King    | 10   | 95
2         | Alan      | Turing  | 11   | 67
3         | Grace     | Hopper  | 10   | 88
4         | Tim       | Lee     | 10   | 42

after: `SELECT` says **which fields**; `FROM` says **which table**; `WHERE` says **which records**. Text values go in **single quotes**; numbers don't. Comparison operators are the usual `= <> < <= > >=` (SQL uses `<>` or `!=` for not-equal).

explain.code:
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE Surname LIKE 'H%';    -- starts with H  (% = any characters)
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE FirstName LIKE '%a%'; -- contains an a
SELECT * FROM Students ORDER BY Score DESC;        -- highest first (ASC is the default)
SELECT FirstName, Score FROM Students WHERE Year = 10 ORDER BY Surname;

p: You'll be given a table and a query and asked what it returns (write out the rows/fields), or given a requirement and asked to write the query. Checklist: right fields after SELECT, right table, the WHERE condition exactly matches the words of the question (over 70 is `> 70`, at least 70 is `>= 70`), quotes round text, `ORDER BY` if the question says 'in order of'.
A table is like a spreadsheet. Each row is a **record** (one student). Each column is a **field** (name, year, score).

simple.code: SELECT FirstName, Score FROM Students WHERE Year = 10;
after: `SELECT` = which columns. `FROM` = which table. `WHERE` = which rows. Put text in 'single quotes'.

simple.code:
WHERE Score > 70 AND Year = 10     -- both
WHERE Surname LIKE 'H%'            -- starts with H
ORDER BY Score DESC                -- biggest first

keyterms.def: One row in a table: all the fields about one item.
One column in a table: one piece of data about each record.
A collection of records with the same fields.
Structured Query Language — used to search and manage data in a database.
Which fields / from which table / which records.
Pattern match; % stands for any sequence of characters.

try.title: 1. Run queries on a real table
p: The `Students` table below is loaded into a database in your browser. Run the query, then change it to: all Year 10 students; first names and scores of anyone scoring 80 or more; students whose surname starts with T.
try.schema:
CREATE TABLE Students (StudentID INTEGER, FirstName TEXT, Surname TEXT, Year INTEGER, Score INTEGER);
INSERT INTO Students VALUES (1,'Ada','King',10,95),(2,'Alan','Turing',11,67),(3,'Grace','Hopper',10,88),(4,'Tim','Lee',10,42),(5,'Katherine','Johnson',11,79),(6,'Linus','Torvalds',10,73),(7,'Margaret','Hamilton',11,91),(8,'Guido','van Rossum',10,58);

try.title: 2. AND, OR, ORDER BY
p: Write queries for: (a) Year 11 students with a score under 80; (b) students called Ada or Grace; (c) everyone, highest score first; (d) Year 10 surnames in alphabetical order.
try.schema:
CREATE TABLE Students (StudentID INTEGER, FirstName TEXT, Surname TEXT, Year INTEGER, Score INTEGER);
INSERT INTO Students VALUES (1,'Ada','King',10,95),(2,'Alan','Turing',11,67),(3,'Grace','Hopper',10,88),(4,'Tim','Lee',10,42),(5,'Katherine','Johnson',11,79),(6,'Linus','Torvalds',10,73),(7,'Margaret','Hamilton',11,91),(8,'Guido','van Rossum',10,58);
try.code: SELECT * FROM Students WHERE Year = 11 AND Score < 80;

try.title: 4. A different table
p: A library table. Write queries for: books by Pratchett; books published before 1950, oldest first; titles containing the word 'the'; the count of books per genre (stretch: `SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) FROM Books GROUP BY Genre`).
try.schema:
CREATE TABLE Books (BookID INTEGER, Title TEXT, Author TEXT, Year INTEGER, Genre TEXT, OnLoan INTEGER);
INSERT INTO Books VALUES (1,'Mort','Pratchett',1987,'Fantasy',1),(2,'The Hobbit','Tolkien',1937,'Fantasy',0),(3,'Dune','Herbert',1965,'Sci-Fi',0),(4,'Guards! Guards!','Pratchett',1989,'Fantasy',0),(5,'1984','Orwell',1949,'Dystopia',1),(6,'The Martian','Weir',2011,'Sci-Fi',0),(7,'Brave New World','Huxley',1932,'Dystopia',0);
try.code: SELECT Title, Year FROM Books WHERE Author = 'Pratchett';

exam.q: A table `Products` has fields ProductID, Name, Price, Stock. Write an SQL query to display the Name and Price of all products with fewer than 5 in stock.
exam.commentary: One mark per clause. `< 5` not `<= 5` — 'fewer than'. Selecting `*` loses the first mark because the question named the fields.

exam.q: Using the Students table shown in this lesson, state what the following query returns.
exam.code: SELECT FirstName FROM Students WHERE Year = 10 AND Score > 80;
model: The first names only (1): Ada and Grace (1).
exam.commentary: State the *field* returned as well as the values. Students who list surnames or whole rows lose the first mark.

exam.q: Identify and correct the error in this query, which should return all books published after 2000: `SELECT * FROM Books WHERE Year > '2000';`
model: Year is a number so should not be in quotes / `'2000'` is text (1). Corrected: `SELECT * FROM Books WHERE Year > 2000;` (1).
exam.commentary: Some databases tolerate it, but the mark scheme treats quotes round a number as the error. Identify, then rewrite.

home: Design a table for your own music or games collection with at least five fields and eight records (write it out). Then write five SQL queries a friend might want to run on it, with the result of each.
